Question 15:
Listen to two people discussing the Volunteer in a clean-up program. Read the opinions below and decide whose opinion matches the statements, the man, the woman, or both the man and the woman. You can listen to the discussion twice.

(Man start)

Man: I watched a news report about the clean-up program yesterday. To be honest, I think the media made it sound much more successful than it really was.

Woman: I agree. They only showed the best parts and ignored many problems. The benefits of the program were clearly exaggerated.

Man: Exactly. And even with programs like this, I still think littering will always be a problem. Some people just do not care enough about public places.

Woman: Maybe, but I don't think we should give up. Volunteers can still make a difference.

Man: That's true, but the problem will never completely disappear.

Woman: For me, the reason why volunteers join is not very important as long as the trash is picked up. Some people say that those who join only want to look good on social media. Whether they do it because they care about the environment or because they want experience, the result can still be the same if they work hard.

Man: I beg to differ. If they don't care genuinely, they will stop doing it soon. In my opinion, instead of relying on fake volunteers, the authorities must implement strict

punishments like heavy fines. That is the only truly effective way to stop people from littering

Woman: I'm not sure it is the best way. Fines might help, but education is also important.

Man: Education helps, but without fines or punishment, many people will not change their behavior.


⟦0⟧ - Media exaggerates the benefits of the programme

⟦1⟧ - Littering will always be a problem

⟦2⟧ - The volunteers’ motivations do not affect the programme outcome

⟦3⟧ - Punishment is the most effective way to prevent littering

I felt completely amazed by the beauty of nature under the sea and realized how relaxing it was just to watch these creatures in their own environment. Person C

sections.name: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

items.h:
TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION (XÁC SUẤT 15%)

For centuries, business models were anchored in physical spaces and tangible goods. But when technology started dissolving the walls of shops and replacing ownership with constant access, the ground shifted. Companies that once sold products now offer experiences and continuous connections. A rented film has morphed into an endless streaming library, and a one-time transaction into a subscription. This evolution reveals a deeper truth: innovation is no longer a supplement but the very skeleton of commerce. To survive, firms must weave digital tools into their core fabric, or risk being left behind.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

Workplaces no longer hum only with human voices; they now share space with silent partners made of code and circuits. These systems shoulder repetitive chores—scheduling, number crunching, data entry—allowing people to redirect their energy toward more creative pursuits. Factories report greater precision, offices experience faster decisions, and the promise of scale feels closer than ever. Yet even allies can unsettle: if workers are unprepared, the same tools that lighten the load may instead spark unease. The challenge is to ensure that automation enhances productivity without draining morale.


.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

A society rushing forward on a digital highway cannot afford passengers who lack the map. Coding, cybersecurity, and data analysis are no longer specialist luxuries but essential literacy. Schools blend these subjects with traditional lessons, and governments pour resources into academies meant to bridge gaps. For citizens, this lifelong education is both shield and passport, protecting them from exclusion while opening doors to opportunity. Without such preparation, technology risks creating a privileged few who sprint ahead and many others stranded on the roadside.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

 When organizations lean too heavily on machinery of logic, cracks begin to show. Algorithms, celebrated for their speed, sometimes replicate human bias in hidden ways. Automated hiring tools might quietly filter out strong candidates; predictive systems may fail spectacularly when conditions change. The more humans surrender decision-making, the more their own judgment dulls, like muscles left unused. Balance, then, is the key: machines can be efficient assistants, but wisdom lies in keeping people firmly at the helm to steer when formulas falter.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

The digital revolution opens doors, but each door also invites intruders. Hospitals frozen by ransomware, schools paralyzed by stolen data—such headlines reveal how fragile online systems can be. What once seemed a purely technical nuisance has grown into a strategic threat that can cripple entire sectors. Protecting networks now requires not only firewalls and passwords, but also culture, training, and swift response plans. Without them, the gains of digital adoption may dissolve into distrust, leaving behind not progress but financial loss and reputational scars.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

Technology’s promise shines brightest when it does not belong solely to the powerful. Broadband in rural towns, free Wi-Fi in public squares, and collaborative platforms for small enterprises—all of these initiatives aim to ensure no one is excluded from the digital age. When ecosystems are designed inclusively, innovation becomes a shared endeavor, not a private privilege. But this requires effort: corporations and governments must look beyond profit to consider communities at the margins, where a single connection can change countless futures.

TOPIC: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION

Every new tool whispers questions beyond its function. Who owns the data? Whose rights are safeguarded, and whose are overlooked? Artificial intelligence may quicken decisions, but it can also entrench inequality if unchecked. Some firms now adopt codes of fairness, attempting to weigh social impact alongside profit margins. Trust, once broken, is difficult to rebuild; yet trust is exactly what sustains long-term innovation. Ethical reflection is therefore not decoration but foundation—ensuring that digital progress uplifts rather than exploits.

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY ver CHÍNH

A. Brilliance does not always guarantee recognition. Many women in mathematics produced groundbreaking work that was published under male names or credited to mentors instead of themselves. Their gender, rather than their ability, dictated how their contributions were received. Some waited decades before their theories were acknowledged, while others were forgotten entirely. These lost voices remind us that the history of mathematics is incomplete—not because women were absent, but because their presence was systematically obscured by prejudice.

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY VER CHÍNH

B. In rare moments, individual women broke through the silence and earned lasting admiration. Ada Lovelace, for example, envisioned algorithms long before the invention of the modern computer. Her notes on Charles Babbage’s analytical engine revealed insights that were centuries ahead of their time. Unlike many of her contemporaries, her work was preserved and celebrated, making her a pioneer recognized across history. Her story highlights how acknowledging a single trailblazer can inspire generations, proving that one example of recognition can carry influence far beyond its own era.
o: Attempting to create a gender balance
Labels can change perspective on people

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY ver chính

  C. For centuries, men benefited from structures that ensured their dominance. Universities barred women from study, societies refused their membership, and when collaborative research appeared, male names were usually placed first. Even mediocre male mathematicians could rise quickly, while women of extraordinary ability were slowed or excluded. This unfair credit system distorted perceptions of talent, making it seem as though mathematics belonged to men alone. In reality, many women’s efforts were hidden behind the inflated reputations of their male peers.
o: Attempting to create a gender balance

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY VER CHÍNH

D.  Some women, despite obstacles, managed to sustain careers of remarkable depth. Emmy Noether, for instance, transformed abstract algebra and theoretical physics, influencing entire fields through her ideas. Her journey was not straightforward—she faced years of rejection and only temporary appointments—but her intellectual power ensured that her work could not be ignored forever. A long career of exceptional brilliance showed that women were not occasional contributors but central figures whose ideas shaped mathematics as profoundly as those of their male counterparts.
o: Attempting to create a gender balance
A long career showing exceptional ability
Labels can change perspective on people

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY VER CHÍNH

E.  The way society labels individuals often defines how their abilities are perceived. For a long time, women were cast as “unsuited” for rigorous subjects, while men were labeled “natural” mathematicians. These labels shaped expectations, narrowing opportunities for one group while elevating the other. Over time, however, shifting perspectives revealed the weakness of such assumptions. As women demonstrated skill equal to men, labels began to change. What was once seen as a fixed truth proved to be nothing more than a cultural invention waiting to be dismantled.

items.h:

F.  In recent decades, initiatives have sought to close the gender gap in mathematics. Scholarships, mentorship programs, and policies encouraging female representation have all contributed to gradual progress. Universities now highlight role models and provide supportive environments for women pursuing advanced study. Although disparities remain, attempts to create gender balance have redefined what is possible. The aim is not charity but fairness: ensuring that talent, wherever it is found, can thrive without being silenced by outdated expectations.

items.h:
TOPIC: GENDER EQUALITY

G. While striving for equality, it is also important to recognize that identical treatment does not always result in fairness. Expecting women to follow the same rigid paths as men once did may ignore their distinct challenges and perspectives. True progress acknowledges diversity of experience, creating flexible systems that value multiple approaches. Uniformity can silence differences; inclusivity, by contrast, allows them to enrich the discipline. In this sense, the goal is not to make every journey the same, but to ensure that every voice is given space to be heard.

TOPIC: MOUNTAIN

For centuries, towering peaks were treated as silent opponents in a contest of strength. To plant a flag on the summit was to declare victory over nature itself. Yet this image is slowly fading. Many climbers now describe mountains less as enemies and more as companions—spaces for thought, culture, and fragile ecosystems. The vocabulary of conquest has given way to that of respect. A climb is no longer measured only by height gained, but by insight and connection found along the way.

Long after they return, climbers carry the memory as a reminder that persistence can transform impossible walls into unforgettable horizons.

The expectation of new records or riskier attempts can weigh heavily. What began as personal exploration may, under society’s gaze, become performance—measured not by meaning, but by applause.

Harsh landscapes often draw people closer together. Nights in cold tents foster trust, and shared struggles turn strangers into lifelong friends. Beyond the rope teams, cultures rooted in mountain valleys speak of peaks as sacred guardians, symbols woven into stories and rituals. For many, the relationship is not conquest but coexistence—learning to respect the generosity of the land while acknowledging its dangers. This bond, forged in hardship and tradition, reveals a human need to belong to something larger than ourselves.

Stability means careful preparation, physical discipline, and the wisdom to step back when conditions turn. sections.name: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

For generations, people have marched to the same rhythm: start on Monday, endure five steady beats, and pause only when Saturday arrives. This pattern has guided schools, transport, and even family life. Yet rhythms can grow outdated, just like a once-popular song that no longer fits the mood. With technology reshaping communication and growing concern for well-being, many argue that the old cadence of five working days no longer serves its purpose. The idea of working only four days each week is thus presented less as an experiment than as a natural evolution of the score.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

When companies tested shorter weeks, the results sounded almost too good to be true. Staff returned from their extended weekends with sharper focus and steadier energy, reporting fewer sick days and greater enthusiasm. Some said they finally had time to cook, to exercise, or simply to breathe. Employers noted that tasks were not neglected but often completed with greater efficiency. Rather than shrinking output, the extra day of rest seemed to sharpen the tools of the mind. These findings suggest that a leaner schedule may paradoxically create richer outcomes for both people and organizations.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

Still, every advantage carries a cost. If wages remain the same but hours fall, then someone must shoulder the difference. For large firms, this may mean hiring more staff; for small businesses, it may mean higher prices or reduced investment. Governments worry, too, about weaker tax revenues should productivity slip. Even loyal customers may grow impatient if services are unavailable on certain days. The ledger of the four-day week, therefore, is not written only in happier employees but also in heavier expenses—an equation that some fear may not balance.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

 Supporters often promise balance, but reality can lean the other way. When tasks designed for five days are packed into four, the pace accelerates. Workers speak of meetings crowding their calendars and deadlines chasing them more aggressively. The extra day off sometimes feels like a mirage, cancelled out by the fatigue of longer shifts. Those who value a steady routine may find the constant compression unsettling. Without careful redesign, the dream of harmony may collapse into exhaustion, proving that fewer days do not automatically mean lighter burdens.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

The structure of five working days has left deep grooves in daily life. Schools open and close in tune with it; buses and trains follow its rhythm; even social traditions cling to its shape. Asking people to step out of this pattern is like asking them to walk off a well-trodden path into uncertain terrain. Many hesitate, fearing disruption not only at work but also at home. Transforming such an ingrained system requires patience, because resistance often comes not from logic but from the comfort of long-standing familiarity.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

What appears to be liberation can, for some, feel like captivity. The compressed schedule demands sustained attention, as if workers are asked to sprint four marathons back-to-back. Days become dense with meetings and tasks, leaving little room to pause. By Friday evening, exhaustion may outweigh the pleasure of the promised extra day off. The fairness of such an arrangement is therefore questioned: a gift of time that, paradoxically, takes more than it gives. Only by redesigning workload carefully can employers ensure that relief is genuine rather than illusory.
o: A way of life now outdated

items.h:
TOPIC: FOUR DAY WORKWEEK

Because no single remedy suits every patient, some experts urge flexibility. Rather than imposing a uniform four-day rule, they propose models shaped by context: flexible hours, seasonal shifts, or simple permission to leave once essential tasks are done. In these experiments, the focus moves from counting days to valuing productivity. The message is clear: what matters is not the calendar itself but the quality of life it enables. Diverse approaches may, in the end, serve the common purpose of building healthier and more sustainable ways of working.
o: A way of life now outdated
